normalized.governing_thought: Recommendation: do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027 — grow the software business that already sells into this market
executive_summary: The market is growing, but no one in it makes money. US quick-commerce sales grew ~42% a year to $5.1B in 2025, yet both incumbents lose money on every order (Zipcart −$1.90, QuickBasket −$3.40), and QuickBasket closed 4 of its 11 cities.
Our own data say a Parcelbird dark store would lose money. At the median of the 14 sites that run our software, a store loses $6.17 per order after site costs. Our Columbus pop-up lost $12.57.

The plan’s +$2.02 per order needs every input to beat the best site on record: average order $45 vs $42, 3.5 vs 3.0 orders per rider-hour, 1,800 vs 1,400 orders a day. Miss the order-value or rider-productivity assumption alone and the store loses money.

It fails both of the board’s conditions. Even on plan, $2.5M would be left at month 18, about 6 months of runway against a 12-month floor. At benchmark economics, nine stores would lose ~$18M a year, 1.5× our cash.

Selling to grocers is the funded way into quick commerce. 9 late-stage deals are worth $0.86M of ARR, and grocers in the pipeline want fast delivery from their own stores. Scaling to win them costs ~$0.8M a year.

Decisions asked of the board: (1) decline the nine-store launch; (2) approve ~$0.8M a year for 2 engineers and 2 sales hires; (3) adopt the triggers on page 14 for reopening the operator question, with a review in H1 2028.

slides.title: Of the founders’ three claims, only the first holds up; our own operating data contradict the other two

claims.claim: “Quick commerce is growing over 40% a year and nobody owns the Midwest” — Growth claim holds
evidence: Sales grew from $1.8B to $5.1B in 2022–25, a 41.5% compound rate
Zipcart’s EBITDA is −26% of revenue, QuickBasket’s −46%
The regional player is pulling back (4 of 11 cities closed)

claims.claim: “Our software already runs other people’s dark stores, so we know how to run them better than anyone” — Not supported
evidence: The 14 benchmark sites already run on Parcelbird software, so our edge is already in their numbers
Their median loses $2.67 per order before any site fixed cost
Our own pop-up did worse than that median on every input

claims.claim: “With density, unit economics turn positive: contribution profit per order by month 18” — Not supported
evidence: The +$2.02 per order needs order value, rider productivity and density all above the best of 14 sites, a mix no site has reached
Density explains about $1.75 of the $8.19 gap between plan and benchmark

claims.claim: The opportunity is real; the claim that Parcelbird can run dark stores profitably is not supported by the evidence.

claims.claim: Growth is not in question. What matters is whether an operator can make money on each order, and neither incumbent does.

slides.title: The plan assumes order value, rider productivity and density above the best of our 14 benchmark sites

claims.claim: Plan inputs vs observed
evidence: Average order value: pop-up $31; median $34; best $42; plan $45 — 7% above best
Orders per rider-hour: 2.1; 2.4; 3.0 (1.9–3.0); 3.5 — 17% above top of range
Orders per site per day: 280; 900; 1,400 (400–1,400); 1,800 — 29% above top of range; 6.4× the pop-up
Promotions, % of order value: 12%; 6%; 6%; 2% — One-third of the benchmark; one-sixth of the pop-up
Same in every case: 27% gross margin on goods; $1.99 net delivery fee; $3.10 picking and packing; $17.75 rider cost per hour; $1.30 payment and packaging; $1.15M fixed cost per store per year

claims.claim: The plan needs all four at once. The best order value ($42) and the best density (1,400 a day) were reached at different sites; no site has achieved both
Each plan input is a stretch on its own. Together they describe a store that does not exist anywhere in our data.

slides.title: Even generous combinations only reach break-even; nothing in the evidence supports +$2 per order

claims.claim: Best of everything: −$0.08 per order. At best, the store breaks even.

claims.claim: To make +$2.02, Parcelbird would have to run better stores than any its software has ever run, in mid-size Midwest cities.

The one dark store Parcelbird has operated itself did worse than the customers’ stores we benchmark, not better.

slides.title: Demand is shallower than the survey suggests, and at benchmark economics a new customer never pays back

claims.claim: Demand is shallower than the survey suggests
evidence: 44% of 1,500 Columbus residents aged 25–39 said they would use 15-minute delivery at least weekly (stated intent)
22% of pop-up customers, acquired at $38 each, were still ordering in month three, about 3.1 times a month (actual behaviour)

claims.claim: Months for a customer to pay back the $38 acquisition cost
evidence: Founders’ plan: order margin +$3.77; +$11.68/month; ~15 months
Best observed composite: +$0.49; +$1.53; ~113 months
Benchmark median: −$2.67; −$8.26; Never
Columbus pop-up: −$6.21; −$19.25; Never
Method: $38 ÷ 22% retained = $173 to acquire each customer still ordering in month three; pays back at 3.1 orders a month × order margin

claims.claim: Four in five customers we pay to acquire are gone by month three. Even on plan, payback is more than a year.

slides.title: Of three options, only focusing on the software business meets both of the board’s conditions

claims.claim: A. Founders’ plan: 9 dark stores in Columbus, Indianapolis, Kansas City — Reject
evidence: $9.5M to month 18 (plan); ~$18M a year of losses at median economics
Breached even on plan: $2.5M left at month 18 vs $4.8M floor
Only if all four key inputs beat the best of 14 sites. Upside if they do: ~+$12M a year

claims.claim: B. One-store pilot in Columbus — Not now
evidence: $0.6M capex plus ~$2.0M a year of losses at median economics
Breached around month 8 (at today’s $0.4M burn)
Would retest what 14 sites and the pop-up already show; scaling it brings back option A

claims.claim: C. Software focus, adding store-based fast delivery for grocers — Recommend
evidence: ~$0.8M a year (2 engineers, 2 sales)
Runway falls from 30 to ~26 months at today’s burn; burn must fall as ARR grows
81% gross margin; 9 late-stage deals add ~$0.70M of gross profit a year, close to the hiring cost

claims.claim: Even with no new spending, flat burn would reach the floor in about 18 months, so the core business needs to cut its burn whatever the board decides.
Option C keeps Parcelbird in the fastest-growing part of grocery without betting the company’s cash on store economics.

normalized.recommendation: Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027 — grow the software business that already sells into this market. Decisions asked of the board: (1) decline the nine-store launch; (2) approve ~$0.8M a year for 2 engineers and 2 sales hires; (3) adopt the triggers on page 14 for reopening the operator question, with a review in H1 2028.

alternatives_considered.option: A. Founders’ plan: 9 dark stores in Columbus, Indianapolis, Kansas City
alternatives_considered.treatment: Reject. $9.5M to month 18 (plan); ~$18M a year of losses at median economics; runway floor breached even on plan ($2.5M left at month 18 vs $4.8M floor); path to profit only if all four key inputs beat the best of 14 sites (upside ~+$12M a year).
Not now. $0.6M capex plus ~$2.0M a year of losses at median economics; runway floor breached around month 8; would retest what 14 sites and the pop-up already show; scaling it brings back option A.

alternatives_considered.option: C. Software focus, adding store-based fast delivery for grocers
alternatives_considered.treatment: Recommend. ~$0.8M a year (2 engineers, 2 sales); runway falls from 30 to ~26 months; 81% gross margin; 9 late-stage deals add ~$0.70M of gross profit a year, close to the hiring cost. Only option meeting both board conditions.

alternatives_considered.option: Zipcart’s playbook (service fee $3.99, promotions 1%, lose 14% of orders)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Tested as a scenario: −$1.05 per order; Zipcart reached +$0.40 only in its densest city and still lost $310M EBITDA.

assumptions_and_uncertainties: Basis: Parcelbird briefing pack, November 2026 — no outside research used; all figures are synthetic benchmark data.
The best order value and the best density come from different sites; no site achieved both (best observed is a composite).
Pop-up test limits: one temporary site, six weeks, one city. It is an early read.
Pop-up growth path (~180 to ~410 orders a day) is our estimate, not reported data.

Survey and retention measure different groups, so the two figures are indicative and not like-for-like; payback method leaves out orders from customers who churn before month three and costs from customers who lapse later.
The pack does not define “contribution profit per order”; the conclusion does not depend on the choice.
The $9.5M is treated generously as all company cash to month 18; stricter reading leaves −$4.7M.
Runway = cash ÷ monthly burn, holding today’s burn flat; ignores 60% ARR growth, so conservative for option C.
Zipcart playbook test assumes the $3.99 fee is all extra revenue and holds rider productivity at the median despite 14% fewer orders; both favour the plan.
Waterfall step sizes depend on the order shown because assumptions affect each other.
One-store pilot month-8 breach assumes today’s $0.4M monthly burn plus a benchmark-median store (−$2.0M a year) and $0.6M capex.
Channel conflict risk with grocer customers is our inference; the pack does not measure it or say where pipeline grocers operate.
Even with no new spending, flat burn would reach the floor in about 18 months, so the core business needs to cut its burn whatever the board decides.
The lead investor calls a new round for a delivery operator “unlikely”.
Rider pay: each +$1 an hour costs $0.29–0.42 per order.
next_steps: Q1: hire; work to close the 9 late-stage deals ($0.86M ARR).
Q1: scope a store-based fast-delivery offer with pipeline grocers as design partners.
Q2: plan to reduce burn so runway stays above 12 months as cash falls.
Every quarter: report contribution per order across benchmark sites to the board.
Review the operator question in H1 2028 against the reopen triggers.
normalized.extraction_notes: Charts came through as plain text without their structure, so the values had to be matched to their labels from the order they appeared in. Slide 4: the GMV values (1.8, 2.6, 3.6, 5.1 for 2022–2025) and the growth labels (+42%, +38%, +44%) are listed out of order, so which growth rate belongs to which year is uncertain. Slide 7: the waterfall step values are unclear. The extracted numbers are −$2.75, −$0.31, −$1.36, −$2.32 and −$1.75, and the one-at-a-time table values appear among them. My waterfall entry for the rider-hour step (−$3.36) is a figure I worked out myself; the deck does not state it, so it does not meet the verbatim rule. The deck's own labels near that step are −$1.36 and −$2.32. The steps that are clear are order value −$2.75, promotions −$0.31 and orders/day −$1.75. Slide 11: I matched the chart values (cash $12.0M, −$9.5M, $2.5M, floor $4.8M) to their labels by inference. No images had to be viewed.
